notes.meaning: God told Moses to send twelve men to explore the land of Canaan, one leader from each ancestor's tribe. The people had already asked to send scouts first, as Deuteronomy recalls, and God permitted it. He had already promised them the good land, but He allowed the mission to test their faith and show what was in their hearts.

Moses obeyed the Lord's command and sent the scouts out from the Wilderness of Paran. These men were respected chiefs and family leaders, though not the top princes who managed the whole camp. Choosing prominent leaders gave their report great weight with the people.

The list of scouts begins with Shammua from the tribe of Reuben and Shaphat from the tribe of Simeon. God made sure every tribe had its own witness so that no one could say they were left out. Except for Caleb and Joshua, these men are remembered only for failing to trust God's word.

Next are Caleb from Judah, Igal from Issachar, and Hoshea from Ephraim. Caleb stands out as a man of great faith who trusted the Lord with his whole heart. Hoshea is the trusted helper of Moses whom we know best as Joshua.

The list continues with Palti from Benjamin, Gaddiel from Zebulun, and Gaddi from the tribe of Manasseh, one of Joseph's sons. Each leader carried the responsibility to guide his people into God's promises. Sadly, their lack of faith would soon drag their tribes into open rebellion.

Ammiel represented Dan, and Sethur represented Asher. These men held high rank and had watched God perform mighty miracles in the desert. Even so, they let their eyes rule their hearts instead of trusting God's power.

Nahbi represented Naphtali, and Geuel represented Gad, completing the list of twelve scouts. Every family line across Israel was represented in this crucial mission. All twelve walked through the very same country, but only two saw it through eyes of faith.

Moses gave Hoshea son of Nun a new name and called him Joshua. Hoshea meant a plea for salvation, but Joshua means 'the Lord saves.' Joshua pointed forward to Jesus, whose name is the same in Greek and who saves His people from sin and death.

Moses instructed the men to enter through the southern dry region called the Negev and then push up into the hill country. This was the nearest and most direct path into Canaan. Going through the dry borderlands also helped them travel quietly without raising immediate alarms.

Moses told them to inspect the land, the towns, the trees, and the soil to see if the ground was rich or poor. He also asked them to observe whether the people were weak or strong, and whether they lived in open tents or walled fortresses. He urged them to be courageous and bring back some fruit, since the first grapes were just ripening in late summer.

The scouts explored the whole territory, traveling from the Wilderness of Zin in the south up to Rehob near Hamath in the far north. They walked the entire length of the country God had promised to Abraham. They likely moved in small groups so the locals would not suspect them of being spies.

While passing through the south, they visited Hebron, the ancient town where Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were buried. A clan of tall warriors descended from Anak lived there, which deeply frightened the scouts. The passage notes that Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt, showing how ancient and established the place was.

In a valley near Hebron, the scouts cut down a single cluster of grapes so large that two men carried it on a pole, along with pomegranates and figs. Carrying it on a wooden bar kept the heavy, ripe fruit from being smashed on the long trek back. The Israelites later called that spot the Valley of Eshcol, which means 'cluster,' to remember the incredible fruit they found there.

The scouts returned to the camp after searching the land for forty days. That gave them plenty of time to learn the truth about the country and its defenses. In Scripture, forty days is often a season of testing, and Israel was now about to face a major test of faith.

The scouts arrived back at Kadesh in the Wilderness of Paran and gave their report before Moses, Aaron, and the entire congregation. They held up the fruit they had carried so everyone could see the proof. God had kept His word about the soil, and the people could see it with their own eyes.

The scouts began by telling Moses that the land was indeed flowing with milk and honey, meaning it was rich and fertile. They showed the fruit to prove their words were true. Even the men who doubted God could not deny that His gift was wonderful.

The ten scouts quickly turned to the dangers, warning that the inhabitants were powerful and the cities were massive and walled. They pointed out the fierce descendants of Anak, along with nations like the Amalekites, Amorites, and Canaanites guarding every part of the land. Their gloomy warning took everyone's eyes off the Lord and put them on their enemies.

As panic spread through the camp, Caleb stepped forward and hushed the murmuring crowd before Moses. He boldly declared that Israel should march right in and take the land, because God would certainly give them victory. Caleb spoke with courageous faith, while Joshua stood beside him in firm agreement.

The other scouts argued back at once, insisting that Israel had no chance against such strong enemies. Looking only at human strength, they felt completely outmatched by the Canaanites. By saying it was impossible, they were treating the Almighty God as if He were too weak to keep His word.

To scare the people away from going, the ten spies spread a bad report, claiming the land 'devours its inhabitants.' They exaggerated wildly by saying that all the people there were huge and that the land wore out anyone who lived in it. Fear made them twist the truth and spread panic throughout the whole congregation.

The scouts claimed they saw the Nephilim, an ancient word for legendary giants, and said the sons of Anak came from them. They felt like tiny grasshoppers next to these warriors, and they assumed the locals saw them the same way. Unbelief made the obstacles look huge, but to the Lord even giants are smaller than dust.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars view the mention of the Nephilim as the spies' dramatic exaggeration born of terror, borrowing an ancient legendary term rather than making a literal claim of pre-flood ancestry.
